metadata.title: Feet on Hips Guard Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Feet on Hips Guard in BJJ. Distance management, sweep mechanics, and submission setups. Fundamental open guard with 65% retention rate.

overview:
Feet on Hips Guard Bottom is a fundamental open guard position where the bottom practitioner places both feet on the opponent's hip bones while lying on their back, creating a powerful frame that controls distance and prevents the guard pass. This position serves as both a transitional state and a launch pad for sweeps, submissions, and guard retention strategies. The feet-on-hips position is often one of the first open guard concepts taught to beginners due to its intuitive mechanics and clear defensive structure.

This guard excels at managing distance against standing or kneeling opponents, using the legs as extendable frames to push away pressure and create space for guard recovery or offensive attacks. The position's strength lies in its simplicity and versatility—practitioners can quickly transition to more complex guards like De La Riva, Reverse De La Riva, or Spider Guard, or launch direct attacks through sweeps and submissions. The feet-on-hips configuration also provides excellent hip mobility, allowing the guard player to adjust angles, threaten leg attacks, and maintain positional control even against aggressive passers.

While relatively low risk compared to more committed guard positions, Feet on Hips Guard requires active management of distance and grip fighting to prevent the opponent from controlling the ankles or diving over the frames. Success in this position depends on maintaining proper foot placement on the hip bones (not the thighs or stomach), active hip movement to track the opponent's position, and constant readiness to transition to other guards or attacks when opportunities arise.
state_invariants: Both feet placed firmly on opponent's hip bones (anterior superior iliac spine landmarks) with ball of foot contact creating maximum pushing surface and connection stability
Bottom practitioner's hips elevated off mat with lower back curved, creating space and mobility for hip movement and angle adjustment while maintaining defensive frame integrity
Bottom practitioner's shoulders remain on mat with head neutral or slightly tucked, maintaining base and preventing opponent from driving forward pressure to flatten guard
Arms extended toward opponent's upper body or sleeves for grip fighting, maintaining connection without being pulled forward or allowing opponent to control wrists
Opponent positioned at distance determined by leg extension, unable to achieve chest-to-chest contact or settle weight into bottom player's guard structure
prerequisites: Guard opening from closed guard or initial guard pull position
Opponent standing or in combat base with hips elevated
Successful foot placement on opponent's hip bones before they establish grips
Active hip elevation to create pushing frame with legs
Grip control on opponent's sleeves, pants, or upper body to prevent diving attacks
key_principles: Maintain feet on hip bones (not thighs or stomach) with ball of foot providing maximum pushing surface and directional control
Keep hips mobile and elevated to create constant angle adjustment and prevent opponent from settling weight or achieving static grips
Use legs as active pushing frames rather than passive barriers, constantly adjusting distance and breaking opponent's posture attempts
Grip fight aggressively to prevent opponent from controlling ankles or pant legs, which would compromise the distance management system
Stay ready to transition to other guards (Spider, De La Riva, X-Guard) when opponent attempts to pass or creates openings
Create angles by walking hips laterally while maintaining foot pressure on hips, setting up sweeps and off-balancing opportunities
Combine pushing and pulling forces through coordinated leg extension and grip control to break opponent's balance and posture

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent steps in close to control ankles or drive pressure
Opponent attempts to pass to one side with weight commitment
Opponent grabs sleeves and attempts to control arms while standing
Opponent drives forward aggressively, allowing closed guard recapture
Opponent reaches forward with one arm extended to control distance

decision_tree.condition: If opponent stands tall with upright posture and reaches for pant grips
If opponent drops to combat base attempting to control ankles
If opponent commits weight forward to drive over frames
If opponent circles laterally attempting Toreando pass
If opponent grabs both ankles and attempts to stack

common_errors.error: Placing feet on opponent's thighs instead of hip bones
common_errors.consequence: Reduced leverage and pushing power, allowing opponent to easily control legs and initiate passing sequences
common_errors.correction: Focus foot placement specifically on bony hip landmarks (ASIS), creating maximum structural connection and pushing efficiency

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to flatten to mat with lower back touching ground
common_errors.consequence: Loss of mobility and frame effectiveness, enabling opponent to settle weight and advance guard pass progression
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant hip elevation with active core engagement, creating curved spine position that preserves movement options

common_errors.error: Extending arms rigidly without active grip fighting
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily controls wrists or sleeves, neutralizing upper body defense and creating passing opportunities
common_errors.correction: Keep arms mobile with constant grip fighting, breaking opponent's grips while establishing your own advantageous connections

common_errors.error: Failing to track opponent's movement with hip rotation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent circles to side or back, bypassing frames and achieving dominant passing angles
common_errors.correction: Walk hips continuously to face opponent squarely, adjusting foot pressure and angles to maintain centered defensive structure

common_errors.error: Remaining static in feet-on-hips position without transitioning
common_errors.consequence: Opponent eventually finds grip combinations or passing angles to defeat the guard through persistence
common_errors.correction: Use feet-on-hips as transitional position, constantly threatening sweeps, submissions, or guard changes to prevent opponent settling

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to control ankles without immediate response
common_errors.consequence: Loss of distance management capability and exposure to stack passes, leg weave passes, and other ankle-control-based attacks
common_errors.correction: React immediately to ankle grabs by retracting legs, changing angles, or transitioning to different guard configuration

common_errors.error: Pushing with feet without coordinated pulling with hands
common_errors.consequence: Opponent maintains balanced posture despite leg pressure, preventing effective sweeps or off-balancing
common_errors.correction: Synchronize pushing and pulling forces through simultaneous leg extension and grip manipulation to break opponent's base

training_drills.name: Feet-on-Hips Distance Management
training_drills.description: Partner stands or kneels while bottom player maintains feet-on-hips position. Top partner attempts various grips and passing entries while bottom player focuses on maintaining optimal distance, hip mobility, and foot placement. Emphasize constant adjustment and prevention of ankle control. Start at 50% intensity and gradually increase resistance.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain from Feet-on-Hips
training_drills.description: Bottom player starts with feet on hips and cycles through scissor sweep, pendulum sweep, and hip bump sweep based on partner's reactions. Top partner provides progressive resistance, creating realistic defensive responses. Focus on smooth transitions between sweep attempts without losing distance control or frame integrity.

training_drills.name: Guard Transition Flow
training_drills.description: From feet-on-hips position, bottom player flows through transitions to Spider Guard, De La Riva Guard, X-Guard, and back to feet-on-hips. Partner provides light resistance and attempts various passing approaches. Emphasize maintaining connection and distance throughout all transitions.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting from Feet-on-Hips
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to establish passing grips (ankle control, pant grips, sleeve control) while bottom player fights grips and maintains feet-on-hips structure. Focus on breaking opponent's grips immediately while establishing offensive grips for sweeps. Reset when either player achieves dominant grip position.

training_drills.name: Situational Guard Retention
training_drills.description: Top partner starts with one ankle controlled. Bottom player must recover feet-on-hips position or transition to superior guard position within 30 seconds. Develops urgency and technical responses to common guard passing threats. Rotate through different initial disadvantages (both ankles controlled, stacked position, etc.).

expert_insights.danaher: The feet-on-hips position represents a fundamental application of frame theory in guard play, where we use the legs as primary structural frames to control distance and opponent movement. The critical insight here is understanding that your feet must contact the hip bones—the anterior superior iliac spine—rather than the softer tissue of the thighs or abdomen. This bony landmark provides maximum transmission of force with minimal energy expenditure. From a biomechanical perspective, this position creates a closed kinetic chain where hip extension generates pushing force that travels through the femur, tibia, and into the opponent's pelvis, creating measurable distance that can be maintained or manipulated based on tactical requirements. The sophistication of this position lies not in its complexity but in its versatility as a hub from which multiple guard systems can be accessed. Your feet on the hips should function as mobile contact points rather than rigid posts—constant micro-adjustments in pressure and angle allow you to track opponent movement and prevent the static grips that enable successful passing.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Feet on hips is one of those positions that looks basic but separates competitors at the highest level because of how it's used tactically. When I play this guard, I'm not just pushing—I'm creating a threat matrix where every adjustment forces my opponent into defensive reactions that open sweep or submission opportunities. The key is understanding that feet on hips is a transitional state, not a destination. I'll use it for maybe 2-3 seconds maximum before I'm already threatening a scissor sweep, pendulum sweep, or transitioning to Spider or De La Riva. In competition, if you stay static in feet on hips, good passers will eventually find ankle control or circling angles to defeat it. My approach is constant motion—I'm walking my hips, changing angles, threatening attacks, and forcing my opponent to make decisions under pressure. When they commit to defending one threat, that's when the actual attack comes from a different angle. The feet-on-hips position gives you time and space to set up these combinations, which is why it's so effective even at black belt when you understand how to weaponize it.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Feet on hips is one of those fundamental positions that people underestimate because it looks too simple, but it's actually a launch pad for some of the most dynamic guard games in modern jiu-jitsu. In the 10th Planet system, we use this position as a reset mechanism—when things get scrambled or you lose your preferred guard configuration, feet on hips gives you instant distance control and breathing room to reassess. What I love about this position is the hip mobility it provides. You're not locked into a static structure like closed guard—your hips are free to move in any direction, which opens up creative sweep entries and transition paths that rigid guard systems can't access. The innovation comes from how you combine the pushing frames with unconventional grips and angle creation. Instead of just holding feet on hips and waiting, we teach students to use this position to create momentum—pump the hips, walk laterally, threaten submissions, and flow into more committed guard positions when opportunities arise. The beauty of feet on hips is that it requires minimal energy to maintain but creates maximum options for offensive action, which aligns perfectly with the efficiency principles we emphasize.

metadata.title: Feet on Hips Guard | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Feet on Hips Guard in BJJ. Fundamental open guard position with active distance management. Beginner 45%, Intermediate 60%, Advanced 75% retention rates.

overview:
Feet on Hips Guard is a fundamental open guard position where the bottom player maintains distance control by placing both feet on the opponent's hip bones. This position serves as a cornerstone for modern guard retention and is often the first open guard variation taught to beginners. The feet on hips position creates a strong pushing frame that prevents the opponent from closing distance and initiating passes, while simultaneously providing the guard player with mobility to create angles, off-balance the opponent, and transition to more sophisticated guards.

This guard emphasizes active hip movement and leg dexterity rather than grips alone. By using the feet as active distance managers against the opponent's hips, the practitioner maintains control over engagement distance while keeping their upper body free to manage grips and create attacking opportunities. The position excels at nullifying pressure-based passing attempts and forces the opponent to work around the leg frames, creating openings for sweeps and transitions.

Feet on Hips Guard represents the bridge between closed guard fundamentals and advanced open guard systems. While simple in concept, mastery of this position develops essential skills including hip mobility, distance management, and timing that translate to all open guard variations. It serves as both a defensive retention position when under pressure and an offensive platform for sweeps, triangles, and transitions to more controlling guards.
state_invariants: Both feet actively placed on opponent's hip bones with heels digging into the iliac crest, toes pointing outward to create maximum pushing surface area and prevent slippage during grip fighting
Guard player's hips elevated off the mat with lower back curved, creating space and mobility for hip movement, angle changes, and preventing opponent from flattening or pinning the guard player
Active leg extension maintaining 12-18 inches of distance between torsos, legs bent at approximately 90-120 degrees at the knee to balance pushing power with mobility and quick retraction capability

Opponent in standing or combat base position facing the guard player, unable to close distance due to the foot frames, typically gripping pants, sleeves, or collar while attempting to control or circle
Guard player's shoulders remain on or near the mat with head mobile, upper body maintaining grip fighting capability while legs do the primary work of distance management and off-balancing
prerequisites: Opponent has opened or passed through closed guard, creating separation
Guard player establishes foot placement on hips before opponent secures dominant grips
Sufficient space exists between players to extend legs into framing position
Guard player maintains active hip mobility and is not flattened to the mat
No immediate passing pressure that has already bypassed the leg frames
key_principles: Maintain active foot pressure on hips with toes pointed outward, creating constant pushing frames that manage distance and prevent opponent from stepping forward or driving pressure
Keep hips elevated and mobile off the mat, never allowing hips to flatten or be pinned, as hip movement is essential for creating angles and transitioning
Use grip fighting to break opponent's posture and control while feet manage distance - grips should pull opponent forward as feet push back to create off-balancing tension
Circle and angle hips constantly, never remaining static in one position, making it difficult for opponent to establish stable passing grips or initiate attacks
Transition feet between hips and other guards proactively before opponent can consolidate passing position, using feet on hips as a temporary retention position rather than static guard
Control engagement distance by adjusting leg extension - extend to create space when opponent pressures, retract to close distance when setting up sweeps or attacks

Opponent drops weight forward trying to smash through frames

actions.technique: De La Riva to X-Guard Transition

decision_tree.condition: If opponent secures strong sleeve or collar grips and begins breaking posture down

common_errors.error: Keeping legs fully extended and static without active hip movement or adjustments
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily circles around rigid leg frames or times attacks between leg movements, passing with toreando or leg drag variations
common_errors.correction: Maintain active hip mobility with legs at 90-120 degree angles, constantly adjusting foot pressure and angles to track opponent's movement while keeping frames active

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to flatten to the mat while maintaining foot frames on hips
common_errors.consequence: Loss of hip mobility eliminates ability to create angles or transition, turning dynamic guard into static position easily passed by patient opponent
common_errors.correction: Keep lower back curved and hips elevated off mat at all times, using core engagement to maintain space and mobility even under pressure

common_errors.error: Placing balls of feet or toes on hips instead of heels with proper foot structure
common_errors.consequence: Weak frames easily collapsed by forward pressure, feet slip off hips during grip fighting, and inability to generate sufficient pushing force
common_errors.correction: Dig heels into hip bones with toes pointed outward, creating stable pushing platform that maintains structural integrity under pressure

common_errors.error: Fighting for grips with upper body while neglecting foot frame maintenance
common_errors.consequence: Opponent steps past feet while guard player is distracted with grip fighting, securing dominant passing position before guard player realizes frames are gone
common_errors.correction: Prioritize maintaining foot frames on hips first, then add grip fighting as secondary layer - feet manage distance while grips create opportunities

common_errors.error: Remaining in feet on hips position statically without transitioning to more controlling guards
common_errors.consequence: Patient opponent systematically breaks down foot frames through grip control and eventually establishes dominant passing position
common_errors.correction: Use feet on hips as temporary retention position, actively transitioning to spider guard, de la riva, x-guard, or closed guard before opponent consolidates passing grips

common_errors.error: Pulling opponent forward with grips while simultaneously pushing with feet in same direction
common_errors.consequence: Opposing forces cancel each other out, giving opponent stable base and eliminating off-balancing potential needed for sweeps
common_errors.correction: Create directional tension by pulling upper body one direction while pushing hips opposite direction, breaking opponent's balance and structure

common_errors.error: Keeping both feet on same hip or allowing feet to drift together on centerline
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily steps to undefended side, passing around consolidated leg frames with simple lateral movement
common_errors.correction: Maintain one foot on each hip bone symmetrically, tracking opponent's movement and adjusting both feet independently to maintain bilateral frames

training_drills.name: Feet on Hips Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner stands in front of guard player who maintains feet on hips position. Partner attempts to step past feet and establish passing position while guard player practices hip movement, foot pressure adjustments, and re-establishing frames when broken. Start at 50% speed and gradually increase intensity.

training_drills.name: Hip Circle and Angle Creation
training_drills.description: From feet on hips position, practice circling hips in complete 360-degree rotation while maintaining foot frames on partner's hips. Partner remains relatively stationary while guard player works on mobility and maintaining frames during movement. Focus on keeping hips elevated and feet active throughout rotation.

training_drills.name: Transition Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Starting from feet on hips guard, flow through sequence: feet on hips → spider guard → de la riva → x-guard → back to feet on hips. Partner provides appropriate reactions and grips for each transition. Build muscle memory for entering and exiting feet on hips position smoothly.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting with Frame Maintenance
training_drills.description: Both partners actively grip fight (collar, sleeves, pants) while guard player must maintain foot frames on hips throughout. Partner attempts to break feet off hips while establishing dominant grips. Guard player practices prioritizing frame maintenance over winning grip battles.

training_drills.name: Sweep Setup from Feet on Hips
training_drills.description: From established feet on hips position, practice entering 3-4 different sweeps (scissor, hip bump, elevator, pendulum) in sequence without completing the sweep. Focus on smooth entries, proper grips, and hip positioning for each sweep variation.

expert_insights.danaher: The feet on hips position represents the most fundamental expression of distance management in open guard, and its simplicity belies its crucial importance in guard retention theory. What makes this position particularly valuable from a systematic perspective is that it teaches the essential principle that guard retention is primarily about controlling engagement distance through leg frames, not grip fighting. The feet act as adjustable struts that maintain optimal distance - close enough to off-balance and attack, far enough to prevent the opponent from establishing dominant control. Students must understand that the position is inherently dynamic, not static; the hips must remain elevated and mobile, creating a moving target that forces the opponent to constantly adjust. The biomechanical advantage comes from the ability to generate pushing force through the skeletal structure of the legs against the opponent's hips, which is far more sustainable than muscular grip strength. When teaching this position, emphasize that it serves as a gateway skill - mastery of feet on hips mobility translates directly to all advanced open guard variations because the fundamental principle of using leg frames to manage distance remains constant across spider guard, de la riva, x-guard, and beyond.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Feet on hips is one of those positions that looks simple but becomes incredibly effective when you understand how to use it aggressively rather than defensively. In competition, I use this position as a constant threat generator - my feet aren't just pushing to keep distance, they're actively creating off-balancing moments that set up my sweeps and submissions. The key is understanding that you're not trying to hold this position forever; you're using it to create reactions and capitalize on them immediately. When my opponent tries to step around my feet, I'm already transitioning to de la riva or x-guard. When they try to smash through, I'm elevating them with butterfly hooks or setting up triangles. The biggest mistake I see competitors make is being too passive in this position, just maintaining frames without threatening anything. Against high-level opponents, you need to be constantly changing angles with your hips, creating sweep opportunities, and making them uncomfortable. My go-to attacks from here are the scissor sweep when they stand tall, immediate transition to x-guard when they try to pressure pass, and triangle setups when they reach for grip breaks. The position also works phenomenally well in no-gi because you can't rely on sleeve grips anyway - you're forced to use proper distance management and hip movement, which is exactly what makes the position effective.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Feet on hips is where the journey begins, man - it's the foundation for understanding how your legs can control everything in open guard. What people don't realize is that this isn't just a basic beginner position; it's actually the escape hatch when everything else is failing. When I'm teaching 10th Planet guys, I tell them feet on hips is your reset button - when your rubber guard is being defended, when your lockdown is getting passed, when you need to create some chaos and reset the engagement, you go back to feet on hips and start building from there. The innovation we bring to this position is treating it as part of a flowing system rather than an isolated guard. From feet on hips, we're immediately looking at mission control entries, we're thinking about how to transition to the truck, we're setting up electric chairs. The hip movement skills you develop here directly translate to our entire guard system because everything in 10th Planet is about creating angles and staying mobile. One drill I love is having students practice going from feet on hips to every other open guard position in 10-second intervals - spider, de la riva, x-guard, butterfly, then back to feet on hips. This builds the understanding that no guard is static, everything flows together, and feet on hips is the nexus point where all these positions connect.

metadata.title: Feet on Hips Guard Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Feet on Hips Guard Top position in BJJ. Complete guide covering passing strategies, pressure management, and high-percentage passes with 60-75% success rates.

overview: Feet on Hips Guard Top represents the passing position when facing an opponent who has established feet on your hips as a defensive frame. This is a common open guard scenario where the bottom player uses their feet to create distance and control the pace of engagement. The top player must systematically break down this frame through grip control, pressure application, and strategic positioning. Success in this position requires understanding how to neutralize the pushing power of the legs while maintaining forward pressure and creating passing opportunities. The position demands patience and technical precision, as rushing into passes often results in the bottom player re-establishing their guard or executing sweeps. Effective top players in this position focus on controlling the knees, breaking the frames, and transitioning to more advantageous passing positions.
state_invariants: Bottom player's feet are placed on top player's hips, creating a pushing frame that maintains distance between the two practitioners
Top player maintains upright posture with strong base, typically in combat base or standing position, preventing forward collapse
Top player controls one or both of bottom player's pants at the knees or ankles, working to break the foot-on-hip frames
Bottom player maintains hip mobility and ability to adjust feet placement, using legs as active defensive tools rather than static barriers
prerequisites: Bottom player has established open guard with feet on hips
Top player has disengaged from closed guard or is approaching from standing
Sufficient space exists between both players for the frame to function
Top player maintains balance and base to prevent sweeps
key_principles: Control the knees before attempting to pass - grip fighting at the pants is essential
Maintain constant forward pressure to prevent bottom player from recovering better guards
Break one frame at a time rather than attempting to clear both feet simultaneously
Keep hips low and weight distributed to prevent being pushed backward
Use angle changes and lateral movement to create passing opportunities
Timing is critical - pass when bottom player adjusts their frames
Protect against De La Riva hooks and lasso guards during frame breaking

counter_transitions.trigger: Bottom player attempts to invert or shoot triangle
Bottom player tries to establish De La Riva or reverse De La Riva
Bottom player creates too much space with frames

decision_tree.condition: If bottom player has both feet on hips with strong frames
If bottom player tries to establish sleeve grips for spider guard
If bottom player begins to shoot triangle or omoplata
If bottom player creates excessive distance with frames

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass without controlling the knees first
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player easily re-establishes guard or executes sweeps
common_errors.correction: Establish strong pants grips at the knees before initiating any passing movement

common_errors.error: Standing too upright with poor base
common_errors.consequence: Vulnerable to push sweeps and loss of balance
common_errors.correction: Maintain low, athletic stance with weight distributed evenly and hips engaged

common_errors.error: Allowing bottom player to establish sleeve grips
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player transitions to spider guard or lasso guard with increased control
common_errors.correction: Fight grips aggressively and keep elbows tight to prevent sleeve control

common_errors.error: Rushing the pass without breaking frames
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player pushes you away or off-balances you
common_errors.correction: Methodically break one frame at a time before committing to pass

common_errors.error: Keeping weight too far back
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player maintains distance and can attack with submissions
common_errors.correction: Apply constant forward pressure while maintaining balance

common_errors.error: Ignoring De La Riva hook threats
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player establishes De La Riva and sweeps or takes the back
common_errors.correction: Keep knee line awareness and clear hooks immediately when they appear

training_drills.name: Frame Breaking Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player establishes feet on hips frames. Top player practices controlling knees and systematically breaking frames one at a time. Focus on grip fighting and maintaining pressure. 3-minute rounds, switch roles.

training_drills.name: Toreando Timing Drill
training_drills.description: From feet on hips position, top player waits for bottom player to adjust their frames, then executes toreando pass. Bottom player varies their frame adjustments to create realistic timing windows. Emphasize reading and reacting.

training_drills.name: Passing Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Top player cycles through different passing options (toreando, knee cut, leg drag, long step) from feet on hips position. Bottom player provides moderate resistance. Focus on smooth transitions between passing attempts.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting Specific
training_drills.description: Isolated drill focusing only on grip fighting from feet on hips position. Top player tries to secure pants grips, bottom player tries to establish sleeve or collar grips. Reset every 30 seconds.

expert_insights.danaher: The feet on hips guard represents a fundamental distance management problem that must be solved through systematic grip control and pressure application. The critical insight is that the bottom player's frames are only effective when they can generate pushing power through their legs. By controlling the knees and preventing full extension, you remove their primary defensive tool. The most efficient approach involves establishing pants grips at the knee line, which allows you to manipulate their leg position and create passing angles. Notice that successful passing from this position requires constant forward pressure - you must make the bottom player feel like they are defending rather than attacking. The moment you allow them to dictate the pace, they will begin to establish more sophisticated guard variations like spider guard or De La Riva. Your goal is to methodically break down their frames while maintaining such overwhelming pressure that submission attacks become their only option for creating space.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, I've found that most people waste too much time trying to be gentle with the feet on hips position. The reality is that you need to be aggressive with your passing - grip their pants hard, control their knees, and impose your will. My preferred approach is the toreando pass because it's fast and shuts down most of their attacking options. When you grip both knees and throw their legs to one side, you're passing before they can establish any dangerous guards. The key is timing - you wait for them to push against you, then use their own force to redirect their legs. I'll also mix in knee cuts when they try to play more defensive, because that forces them to choose between defending the pass or setting up attacks. Against high-level guys, I'm constantly changing my passing angle to prevent them from timing my movements. The worst thing you can do is stay static - if you let them set their grips and establish rhythm, now you're playing their game instead of yours.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The feet on hips position is interesting because most people approach it way too traditionally. In the 10th Planet system, we've developed some unconventional ways to deal with this that really mess with people's timing. One thing I love is using the twister pass when they have their feet on my hips - you grab one leg, step over it, and you're immediately in a position to threaten the truck or take the back. Most people aren't expecting that level of aggression from feet on hips position. Another thing we do is immediately threaten the lockdown when we see feet on hips - if you can trap one leg and establish your hook, now they're dealing with a whole different problem. The traditional pressure passing stuff works, but I like to keep people guessing. Sometimes I'll even pull them into my own closed guard from this position if they're being too defensive - now they have to deal with rubber guard and all those submission chains. The point is, don't get stuck in one mindset about what this position is supposed to be.
